## Setup

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(broom)
library(simling)
```

`simling` is an R package of simulated linguistic data. If it is not installed yet, run these two lines once, in the Console:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("mcanzi/simling")
```

## The data {.smaller}

In `agreement_attraction`, 40 participants read sentences like *The key to the cabinet(s) was/were rusty* while an eye tracker records their eye movements. The verb is either grammatical (*was*) or ungrammatical (*were*), and the noun before it, the **attractor**, is singular (*cabinet*) or plural (*cabinets*). `gaze_duration` is the time in ms that readers look at the verb the first time they reach it. It is `NA` when they skipped the verb.

```{r}
glimpse(agreement_attraction)
```

Today's question: does a plural attractor make an ungrammatical verb easier to read?

---

## 1. Two categorical predictors

### 1.1 Four cell means

Compute the mean `gaze_duration` in each of the four combinations of `grammaticality` and `attractor`, and save the result as `cells`. Use `na.rm = TRUE`, because skipped verbs have no gaze duration.

::: solution

```{r}
cells <- agreement_attraction |>
  summarise(gaze = mean(gaze_duration, na.rm = TRUE), .by = c(grammaticality, attractor))
cells
```

:::

### 1.2 An interaction plot

Plot the four means from `cells`, with `grammaticality` on the `x` axis and one colour and one line per `attractor` (`group = attractor`). Are the lines parallel?

::: solution

```{r interaction-plot, eval = FALSE}
cells |>
  ggplot(aes(x = grammaticality, y = gaze, colour = attractor, group = attractor)) +
  geom_point(size = 4) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  xlab("Verb") + ylab("Gaze duration (ms)") +
  theme(legend.position = "right")
```

:::

::: solution

```{r, ref.label = "interaction-plot", echo = FALSE}
```

The lines are not parallel. Ungrammatical verbs are read more slowly, but much less so after a plural attractor.

:::

### 1.3 The model

Fit a linear model of `gaze_duration` with `grammaticality`, `attractor` and their interaction, and print its coefficients. What are the reference levels?

::: solution

```{r}
m <- lm(gaze_duration ~ grammaticality * attractor, data = agreement_attraction)
coef(m)
```

The reference levels are `grammatical` and `singular`, the first level of each factor. The intercept is the mean gaze duration on a grammatical verb after a singular attractor.

:::

### 1.4 Rebuild the cell means

Use the four coefficients to compute the predicted gaze duration in each of the four cells. Compare your numbers with `cells`.

::: solution

```{r}
b <- coef(m)
c(grammatical_singular = b[[1]],
  ungrammatical_singular = b[[1]] + b[[2]],
  grammatical_plural = b[[1]] + b[[3]],
  ungrammatical_plural = b[[1]] + b[[2]] + b[[3]] + b[[4]])
```

The four predictions are the four cell means. The interaction coefficient is only needed for the cell where both predictors differ from their reference level.

:::

### 1.5 In words

Say in two sentences what the coefficient of `grammaticalityungrammatical` and the interaction coefficient mean.

::: solution

After a singular attractor, an ungrammatical verb is read `r round(b[[2]])` ms more slowly than a grammatical one. After a plural attractor, this cost is `r round(abs(b[[4]]))` ms smaller, only `r round(b[[2]] + b[[4]])` ms: the plural attractor makes *were* look less wrong.

:::

---

## 2. A categorical and a continuous predictor

`lexical_decision_l2` has reaction times (`rt`, in ms) of 15 L1 and 15 L2 speakers of German to 40 words, with each word's log10 frequency (`log_freq`).

### 2.1 Two groups, two lines

Plot `rt` against `log_freq`, with one colour and one regression line per `group`. Do frequent words help both groups equally?

::: solution

```{r l2-plot, eval = FALSE}
lexical_decision_l2 |>
  ggplot(aes(x = log_freq, y = rt, colour = group)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  xlab("log10 frequency") + ylab("Reaction time (ms)") +
  theme(legend.position = "right")
```

:::

::: solution

```{r, ref.label = "l2-plot", echo = FALSE}
```

The line of the L2 speakers is steeper: they gain more from frequent words.

:::

### 2.2 Centre and fit

Centre `log_freq` on its mean, in a new column `freq_c`. Fit a model of `rt` with `freq_c`, `group` and their interaction. What do the coefficients of `freq_c`, `groupL2` and the interaction mean?

::: solution

```{r}
lex <- lexical_decision_l2 |>
  mutate(freq_c = log_freq - mean(log_freq))
m_lex <- lm(rt ~ freq_c * group, data = lex)
coef(m_lex)
```

For L1 speakers, each log unit of frequency makes responses `r round(abs(coef(m_lex)["freq_c"]))` ms faster. For a word of average frequency, L2 speakers are `r round(coef(m_lex)["groupL2"])` ms slower than L1 speakers. For L2 speakers, the frequency effect is `r round(abs(coef(m_lex)["freq_c:groupL2"]))` ms larger: responses get `r round(abs(coef(m_lex)["freq_c"] + coef(m_lex)["freq_c:groupL2"]))` ms faster per log unit.

:::

### 2.3 Bonus: without centring

Fit the same model with `log_freq` instead of `freq_c`. Which coefficient changes a lot, and why?

::: solution

```{r}
coef(lm(rt ~ log_freq * group, data = lexical_decision_l2))
```

The coefficient of `groupL2` changes: it is now the difference between the groups for a word with a log frequency of 0, far below the frequencies in the data. Where the lines are steeper, the groups are further apart, so this difference is larger than at the mean frequency. The slopes and the interaction stay the same.

:::
